# PART 3: The Anatomy of Emotional Intelligence — Definition, Self-Rule, and the Five Marks of Its Absence

### Third Sunday — Last Sunday of the Month

## Continuing Where We Left Off

We have covered quite a lot so far, even if I have not yet given a formal definition — and the reason I did not define it first is because I wanted you to have an understanding of what it is before I did. Last time we saw Jesus Himself showcase His intelligence at Gethsemane, where those who should have prayed with Him slept instead — and what a man not so designed could have called betrayal, Jesus looked at and said, "the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." Discernment is where you see beyond what the natural eye can see. We read about Joseph, who was able to forgive the very people who brought calamity into his life, and park all of that aside to focus on the good that came from what he experienced. We were able to ask a very important question: can we be in a position where we ignore the pain that happens to us, and focus on the purposes of God?

Today we continue. I really want to hurry a bit, because this is the last Sunday of the month, and I will not be able to cover everything I wanted to cover in relation to emotional intelligence — I will return to this topic when we talk about relationships (and no, not only romantic relationships). One of the areas I really want to focus on today is communication, because your unintelligence in emotions is normally revealed when you are communicating.

## Defining Emotional Intelligence

So I want to define emotional intelligence. If you're writing, you can say:

> *Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognize, understand, manage, and appropriately express your own emotions, while also discerning and responding wisely to the emotions of others, in ways that build relationships, solve problems, and prevent unnecessary harm.*

And another definition of the same thing:

> *Emotional intelligence is the maturity to remain aware of what is happening within you and around you, allowing your feelings to inform your decisions without controlling them, while treating others with understanding, wisdom, and self-control.*

## Ruling Your Spirit

> *He who is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city.*
> — Proverbs 16:32 (NKJV)

There is such a thing as ruling your spirit — being in charge of what happens inside of you, and in charge of what happens around you. One of the things that shows you are not intelligent emotionally is constant fighting — but we're getting there.

Are you aware the Bible calls *you* a city also? You are a city set on a hill. So when the Bible says "he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city," it means: when the devil wants to overtake you — a city — if you know how to rule your spirit, you find yourself at an advantage. Most times we blame the devil for what we should blame ourselves. Have you seen people lose jobs because of unfiltered speech — "I'm just speaking my mind" — and then come to church and say there is a demon attacking them, that every job they get, they lose within three months? There is no demon there. You just cannot rule your spirit. So when the enemy wants to overtake you, he easily does, because you cannot rule your spirit. There are people who lose every relationship they enter — not because the people they meet are snakes, but because they, themselves, cannot rule their spirit; they have no self-control, so anything that comes to mind, they speak it. It is not that people won't push you to certain extremes — but feeling the necessity to react a certain way is not a justification to react unwisely. The Bible does not say you will never become angry — it says be *slow* to anger.

## Wisdom Over Strength

> *Then I said, "Wisdom is better than strength."*
> — Ecclesiastes 9:16 (NKJV)

When I read this verse, I think of men — because it is men who are strong. There is a way, as men, we can misuse strength and forget wisdom — for example, when men beat their wives, they have remembered strength and forgotten wisdom. When I teach on communication and relationships in future, I'll also teach something on communication across genders — men do not speak the same way as women, and there are things that work in speaking to one that do not work with the other. For example, never criticize a man — it does not work. It works, painfully, for women, but it does not work for men. I'll teach this another time.

## Every Day Is an Audition

This life is very deep. Every single day we walk into minefields of opportunities, interactions, and trials — every person you meet is a test, because life is a complex web of connection, and the tragedy is that most of these connections are unseen. Every room you walk into, every conflict you handle, every authority you encounter, may be a test to your maturity.

> *Behold, I stand here by the well of water, and the daughters of the men of the city are coming out to draw water. Now let it be that the young woman to whom I say, "Please let down your pitcher that I may drink," and she says, "Drink, and I will also give your camels a drink" — let her be the one whom You have appointed for Your servant Isaac.*
> — Genesis 24:13–14 (NKJV)

This is Abraham's servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac. Many daughters of the city are coming to the well — but remember, he's looking for one. Imagine if Rebekah had come that day with a nasty attitude. Imagine, it is you — a stranger comes and says, "Give me a drink, and my camels too" — and even before you say hello back, your first response is, "Who are you, what do you want?" If you have that kind of attitude, get born again today. There are specific credentials you must attain, because there are certain things God cannot do with you unless you attain them.

Write this down: **every day of your life is an audition.** You may be praying, you may be fasting, but your attitude can be a repellent. There is a man — this is what I normally tell men — don't be quick to tell a woman you want to marry her. Stay around, observe her attitude, see how she treats other people. The minute you tell them, they will behave nicely. Before that, watch how they handle conflict, how they treat people who cannot do anything for them. The quality of your life can completely change because of a single moment, a single decision. You can spend ten years building a life, a career, a marriage — and destroy it in ten seconds, because you couldn't master an immediate emotional reaction. Most people believe their success depends purely on their talents, their qualifications — but talents and gifting open the door; **emotional regulation decides whether you stay in that room.**

## The Credential of Self-Control

There was an assignment given to Moses that was given to another because he lacked a certain credential — self-control. God told him, "Go and speak to the stone," and Moses, instead, struck it. For that, God told him he would not lead the people into the Promised Land — Joshua took over. There are things you will miss in life because you are lacking certain credentials, and mostly, they are closely related to emotional intelligence.

Even further — Moses told God, in Exodus, "Send someone else," and the Bible says the anger of the Lord was kindled against him. Do you think God could not have performed a miracle so that Moses would speak well? He did exactly that kind of miracle later with Isaiah, with a coal of fire touching his lips. Why not for Moses? Because God said, "Aaron will go with you; he shall speak, and I will teach *you*." Some of you are asking for a miracle. You need to be taught how to speak.

## The Cost of an Irreversible Moment

I was watching a movie — an honest FBI agent, one of the good ones, not corrupt. His badge is taken because of something that happened, and when he goes to collect it, his senior — a woman — says something so offensive that he strikes her, one motion, and she falls and dies. Now this good cop has to look for someone to help him hide it, because murder is a direct ticket to life imprisonment. He compromised, even as a good cop, because in one moment he did something he could not reverse. He does not know how to resurrect someone.

This is the tragic nature of emotional reaction — most times, it is permanent. Once the word has left your mouth, once the email is sent, once the message is sent, once the bridge is burned, you cannot recall it. **You are left sitting in the ashes of the fire you lit just to warm your ego — for five seconds.**

## Unfiltered Speech Is Not Bravery

We live in a culture that worships unfiltered speech — "I speak my mind," "I say it as it is," "I'm just being real." Let's call this what it is: it is not bravery, it is foolishness. **Unfiltered speech is a mark of an undisciplined mind.** It assumes that everything that comes to your mind needs an audience, that every feeling that comes to your chest needs a microphone. (I'm speaking to the Gen Zs — I am very much aware.) There are people in your life — a family member, a colleague, your boss — who are not going to treat you nicely, who will be difficult, demanding, unfair. But their bad behaviour does not give you permission to ruin your own future. Sometimes we think we know our rights — but who told you that you can express your rights to anyone, anywhere, regardless of who is holding the door you need to enter tomorrow? When your boss tests your patience, **biting your tongue is not cowardice — it is strategic wisdom.**

Some of these difficult people are critically important to your destiny. I remember someone — let's call him a man who worked in one company and lied to his boss about being sick, to go interview at another — only to find, in the interview room, that it was a branch of the same company, and his own boss sitting on the panel. He lost both jobs. You never know when the person you're insulting in traffic, or lying to, is the very one seated in the room of your next decision.

## Why You Don't Fire Everyone Who Frustrates You

Even when you are the boss, there are people you are not meant to fire, no matter how difficult they are — because sometimes they are holding a skill that will push your company, or your destiny, to the next level. I heard a story from a man they call Pastor Apoju — in his office, a woman was causing chaos, and every employee told him, "You need to fire this woman." But he had discernment, and every time he thought of it, he felt a restraint not to. After some time she left, went abroad, and was hired at a television station as a programmer — the one who decides who ministers on air. And it happened that Pastor Apoju was given that very slot — that is how he went, for the first time, to minister on television.

There are people even I have not chased out of ministry when others thought I should — people who have planted scandals against me, and God has shown me before time, and yet I impart grace on them in the next service, and someone is offended, wondering why I am not acting. I have heard people say crazy things about me, and I know they lied — but I don't always tell them I know.

> *He who pampers his servant from childhood will have him as a son in the end.*
> — Proverbs 29:21 (NKJV)

Some of these people, we are bearing them because we want them to become sons in the end. We understand today you are a gossiper, we understand today you are a snake — but we are looking to have you as a son in the end. That is why we don't get tired with certain people. There is a way emotional restraint will allow you to look past the friction and see the bigger picture, and that action might position you for a major breakthrough. **Wisdom knows that not every provocation deserves a response.**

## The Anatomy of Emotional Unintelligence

Let me give you the anatomy — the science — of emotional unintelligence.

**1. Constant fighting.** The easiest thing to do in the flesh is to fight. It requires zero discipline to scream, to slam doors, to trade insults — it takes far less energy to burn a bridge than to build one. When children are growing, in their first years they respond only through impulse — if they're hungry or angry, they cry, they scream — because their minds have not developed to a place where they can judge rightly. That is why we're taken to school: so our minds develop to a point where they can find purpose for our emotions. **True intelligence is the ability to sit down, assess a situation, and talk through it without escalation.**

**2. Reaction over reflection.** A person who is not emotionally intelligent cannot handle honest feedback, no matter how lovingly it is packaged. The moment correction comes, the walls go up. They react with defensiveness instead of reflecting with humility, because they view feedback as an attack on their character rather than an invitation to grow.

**3. Making everything about yourself.** Have you met people who turn every conversation into a competition of suffering? You tell them what you're going through, and they want to compete that theirs is worse — especially about money. What kind of trophy are you looking to inherit? They cannot allow you to express yourself, cannot hear you out, because they're quick to interrupt so they can tell their own story. This is an inability to extend empathy, because you want your own ego validated.

**4. Weaponized history.** When a foolish person is clearly proven wrong, they will never look you in the eye and say, "I'm sorry." Instead, they dig up a ghost from your past: "Is this not the same thing you did to me last year?" They weaponize history because they lack the courage to own their present failure.

**5. Crossing emotional boundaries.** There are people who can't even tell when they're overstepping — they don't know how to read the room, they're missing social cues entirely, with a total lack of awareness of the environment they're in.

## The Closing Charge

The next time you feel the urge to say your mind, or burn a bridge, stop and ask yourself this single question:

> **Am I about to sacrifice ten years of my life, of my future, just to win ten seconds of an argument?**

The last thing I will say: **do not let your emotions draft the script of your life.**

> *Father God, we thank you for being a good God unto us. Thank you for teaching us how to control, how to regulate our emotions. Thank you for being mindful of us. There is no one better than you. You have shown us mercy, and we ask you to give us the same grace to show others mercy. Help us to be kind to others. Help us to see things as you see them. Help us to judge as you judge. In Jesus' mighty name. Amen.*

## Core Declarations of This Teaching

1. **People who are emotionally intelligent end up ruling over people who have a strong IQ and a weak emotional quotient.**
2. **There is a difference between being a believer and being a Christian.** A believer has a ticket to heaven; a Christian is a disciple whose character has become notable — like Christ.
3. **We do not believe you love God by what you say — we believe it by looking at whether you love the people around you.**
4. **The wisdom of God is context-specific.** You can be sharp in business and dull in marriage; excellent in ministry and lacking in raising your own children.
5. **Grace does not erase consequences.** God's kindness still leads us to repentance — even Rahab, even Eli, still lived with the outcomes of their choices.
6. **Discernment is emotional intelligence.** It is the ability to see beyond the action to the motive behind it — the way Jesus saw past His disciples falling asleep in Gethsemane.

2. **Non-scripture claims are never checked at all** — things like "statistically, arranged marriages divorce less" or the movie/anecdote details are preserved as the speaker's own assertions, exactly as spoken. The skill is explicitly anti-summary/completeness-focused, not a claims-verification tool.

If you want real rigor, I can go back through and verify every scripture citation against an actual NKJV text now (I have web access) — just say the word.

194	## Common Pitfalls
195	
196	1. **Trusting numbered file order as chronological order.** The whole reason this skill's
197	   compile prompt exists is that this assumption was wrong in the reference case — Part 1
198	   was not taught first.
199	2. **Iterating filenames-with-spaces via an unquoted bash variable.** Silently mangles paths
200	   and can hang a stray command reading stdin. Always use arrays or a properly quoted glob.
201	3. **Letting the compile step transcribe the speaker's spoken paraphrase as the literal
202	   scripture/source citation.** Look up and quote the real reference text; keep the
203	   paraphrase as the speaker's own commentary in the prose.
204	4. **Summarizing instead of compiling.** The brief explicitly wants completeness ("do not

- **Store the API key outside any git-tracked directory**, `chmod 600`, referenced by path

- **Keep the numbered-parts naming convention (`<Prefix> <N>.<ext>`) consistent** across a
  whole series — every script here depends on it for auto-discovery.

  they're "just context" — they're what makes correct chronological reordering possible
  when the numbered parts alone don't carry enough evidence.

1. **Trusting numbered file order as chronological order.** The whole reason this skill's

   was not taught first.

   and can hang a stray command reading stdin. Always use arrays or a properly quoted glob.

## Purpose

Turn a folder of long raw audio/video recordings (a multi-part sermon/lecture/talk series,
meeting recordings, etc.) into one polished, chronologically-correct, voice-preserving
markdown document — reproducibly, end to end: **split** into manageable chunks, **transcribe**
each chunk via a speech-to-text API, **consolidate** chunks back into one transcript per
source recording, then **compile** all of it into a single publication-quality document using
an LLM with a specific, load-bearing prompt.

`.mp4` files (53–99 minutes each) → 17 stream-copy-split parts → 17 real transcriptions via
the Modulate STT API → 5 consolidated per-session transcripts → 1 compiled 6-session teaching
document with correct chronological reordering (the numbered parts were **not** taught in
1-2-3-4-5 order — the compile step had to figure that out from internal evidence).

---

## When to Use

1	# Compilation Prompt — Consolidated Transcripts → One Chronological Teaching Document
2	
3	This is the prompt that produced a genuinely excellent result the first time (a 5-part
4	"Faith" sermon series compiled into one polished, chronologically-correct, voice-preserving
5	markdown document). Use it verbatim with placeholders filled in, against an LLM chat that
6	takes file attachments — or hand this whole file plus the transcripts to an agent with
7	Write access and ask it to follow §"Structural Rulebook" directly.
8	
9	## What to attach
10	
11	1. All N consolidated part-transcripts from `consolidate-transcripts.sh`
12	   (e.g. `Faith 1.txt` … `Faith 5.txt`).
13	2. Any broader-context recordings that cover the same material inside a wider session —
14	   e.g. full meeting/Google-Meet transcripts, if you have them. These aren't required, but
15	   they're what let the compiling model recover the *true* chronological order and connective
16	   context the numbered parts alone don't carry.
17	
18	## The prompt (fill in the brackets)
19	
20	```
21	Attached are transcripts of a series on [TOPIC] done by [TEACHER/SPEAKER NAME]
22	([N range, e.g. 1-5]).
23	
24	After that, the attached are actual transcripts ([SOURCE, e.g. Google Meet]) from
25	which the [TOPIC] series was taught (broader in context as they cover entire
26	sessions as compared to the [N] parts that only cover the teaching).
27	
28	From the above, generate (compile them into) one teaching on [TOPIC] by [TEACHER
29	NAME]. .md format. In the file, there should be a chronological flow of the
30	[TOPIC] series ([N range] doesn't really reflect the manner in which they were
31	taught — you might find that part 1 was taught after part 4). I think the [N
32	range] parts nail the teaching well, whereas the other transcripts sort of give
33	some context. If [TEACHER NAME] made any prayers/declarations/punchlines/
34	statements be sure to include them in the file, still in a chronological manner.
35	Also all scripture [or: quotes/citations from your authoritative source] to be
36	referenced in [NKJV, or your default translation/edition] unless of course
37	otherwise stated. Format well — headings, titles, bold, italic, etc.
38	
39	This is a professional [TOPIC] document. Do not leave out a thing. Let it be
40	such that it is as if [TEACHER NAME] is speaking directly to whoever reads it.
41	```
42	
43	The load-bearing phrases, and why each one matters (don't drop these when adapting):
44	- **"doesn't really reflect the manner in which they were taught"** — this is the single
45	  instruction that forces real chronological reasoning from internal evidence, instead of
46	  the model lazily trusting the file numbering. Without it, you get parts 1-5 in that literal
47	  order, which is very likely *wrong*.
48	- **"the other transcripts sort of give some context"** — explicitly ranks the two source
49	  types (numbered teaching parts = primary structure/weight; broader recordings = context
50	  filler), so the model doesn't over-weight the noisier, less-curated source.
51	- **"be sure to include them ... still in a chronological manner"** — prayers/declarations/
52	  punchlines are exactly what a lazy summarizer drops first. Naming the category explicitly
53	  is what keeps them in.
54	- **"unless of course otherwise stated"** — the one correctly-scoped escape hatch: don't
55	  force the standard translation over a quote the speaker explicitly attributed elsewhere.
56	- **"Do not leave out a thing"** — sets completeness, not summarization, as the goal. This is
57	  a compile, not a digest.
58	- **"as if [name] is speaking directly to whoever reads it"** — the instruction that produces
59	  first/second-person voice preservation instead of third-person academic paraphrase.
60	
61	---
62	
63	## Structural Rulebook (reverse-engineered from the reference output)
64	
65	If you're generating this directly (an agent with Write access, not a separate chat), follow
66	this structure — it's what the prompt above reliably produces, made explicit:
67	
68	1. **Title block**: H1 title that names the *theme*, not "Compiled Transcript" (e.g. "The
69	   Life of Faith"). H2 "A Teaching Series by [Name]". H3 venue/series line. Bold date range.
70	   Horizontal rule.
71	2. **Epigraph**: the 1-2 scripture/quotes most central to the whole series, blockquoted,
72	   italic verse text, em-dash citation, translation noted — set before any narrative content.
73	3. **"A Note Before We Begin"**: an introductory framing section in the speaker's own first-
74	   person voice, drawn from their *actual opening remarks in the chronologically-earliest
75	   session* — not a generic AI-written preamble. If the earliest session has no natural cold

# Compilation Prompt — Consolidated Transcripts → One Chronological Teaching Document

This is the prompt that produced a genuinely excellent result the first time (a 5-part
"Faith" sermon series compiled into one polished, chronologically-correct, voice-preserving
markdown document). Use it verbatim with placeholders filled in, against an LLM chat that
takes file attachments — or hand this whole file plus the transcripts to an agent with
Write access and ask it to follow §"Structural Rulebook" directly.

## What to attach

1. All N consolidated part-transcripts from `consolidate-transcripts.sh`
   (e.g. `Faith 1.txt` … `Faith 5.txt`).
2. Any broader-context recordings that cover the same material inside a wider session —
   e.g. full meeting/Google-Meet transcripts, if you have them. These aren't required, but
   they're what let the compiling model recover the *true* chronological order and connective
   context the numbered parts alone don't carry.

## The prompt (fill in the brackets)

```
Attached are transcripts of a series on [TOPIC] done by [TEACHER/SPEAKER NAME]
([N range, e.g. 1-5]).

After that, the attached are actual transcripts ([SOURCE, e.g. Google Meet]) from
which the [TOPIC] series was taught (broader in context as they cover entire
sessions as compared to the [N] parts that only cover the teaching).

From the above, generate (compile them into) one teaching on [TOPIC] by [TEACHER
NAME]. .md format. In the file, there should be a chronological flow of the
[TOPIC] series ([N range] doesn't really reflect the manner in which they were
taught — you might find that part 1 was taught after part 4). I think the [N
range] parts nail the teaching well, whereas the other transcripts sort of give
some context. If [TEACHER NAME] made any prayers/declarations/punchlines/
statements be sure to include them in the file, still in a chronological manner.
Also all scripture [or: quotes/citations from your authoritative source] to be
referenced in [NKJV, or your default translation/edition] unless of course
otherwise stated. Format well — headings, titles, bold, italic, etc.

This is a professional [TOPIC] document. Do not leave out a thing. Let it be
such that it is as if [TEACHER NAME] is speaking directly to whoever reads it.
```

The load-bearing phrases, and why each one matters (don't drop these when adapting):
- **"doesn't really reflect the manner in which they were taught"** — this is the single
  instruction that forces real chronological reasoning from internal evidence, instead of
  the model lazily trusting the file numbering. Without it, you get parts 1-5 in that literal
  order, which is very likely *wrong*.
- **"the other transcripts sort of give some context"** — explicitly ranks the two source
  types (numbered teaching parts = primary structure/weight; broader recordings = context
  filler), so the model doesn't over-weight the noisier, less-curated source.
- **"be sure to include them ... still in a chronological manner"** — prayers/declarations/
  punchlines are exactly what a lazy summarizer drops first. Naming the category explicitly
  is what keeps them in.
- **"unless of course otherwise stated"** — the one correctly-scoped escape hatch: don't
  force the standard translation over a quote the speaker explicitly attributed elsewhere.
- **"Do not leave out a thing"** — sets completeness, not summarization, as the goal. This is
  a compile, not a digest.
- **"as if [name] is speaking directly to whoever reads it"** — the instruction that produces
  first/second-person voice preservation instead of third-person academic paraphrase.

---

## Structural Rulebook (reverse-engineered from the reference output)

If you're generating this directly (an agent with Write access, not a separate chat), follow
this structure — it's what the prompt above reliably produces, made explicit:

1. **Title block**: H1 title that names the *theme*, not "Compiled Transcript" (e.g. "The
   Life of Faith"). H2 "A Teaching Series by [Name]". H3 venue/series line. Bold date range.
   Horizontal rule.
2. **Epigraph**: the 1-2 scripture/quotes most central to the whole series, blockquoted,
   italic verse text, em-dash citation, translation noted — set before any narrative content.
3. **"A Note Before We Begin"**: an introductory framing section in the speaker's own first-
   person voice, drawn from their *actual opening remarks in the chronologically-earliest
   session* — not a generic AI-written preamble. If the earliest session has no natural cold
   open, use its first substantive paragraph.
4. **One "# PART [ordinal]: [session's own descriptive title]" section per distinct session**,
   in true chronological order, each carrying:
   - H3 date of that session (only if the source states or clearly implies one — don't invent
     dates)
   - H2 thematic subheadings for each major movement of thought
   - H3 subheadings tied to specific source-passages taught, each immediately followed by
     the passage **quoted from the real reference text** (see Common Pitfalls — not the
     speaker's paraphrase) in a blockquote with citation
   - Body prose that preserves the speaker's actual phrasing, rhetorical repetition, and
     idiom — paraphrase as little as humanly possible; this is a transcript compile, not a
     summary
   - **Bold** for the speaker's key doctrinal/declarative one-liners
   - Blockquotes (same `>` syntax as scripture) for standout verbatim quotes, illustrative
     asides, and personal anecdotes — visually distinct from body prose
   - A dedicated callout subsection for any ritual/ceremonial moment (e.g. "## Communion
     Declaration — [date]"), with the prayer/declaration text preserved close to verbatim
5. **Closing section**: the final prayer/declaration from the chronologically-last session,
   verbatim, blockquoted.
6. **Summary table**: `| Session/Date | Theme | Key Scripture |`, one row per PART, in
   chronological order.
7. **"Core Declarations" list**: 8-10 numbered, pithy one-line doctrinal takeaways distilled
   from across the whole series — these are for skimming/reference, not new content.
8. **Closing pull-quote**: the single most memorable line from the whole series, blockquoted
   with attribution.
9. **Footer**: italic attribution block — compiled-from note, organization, date range,
   speaker name.

### Voice rules
- First person ("I") when the speaker refers to themself; second person ("you") when they
  address the audience directly. The reader should feel spoken to, not informed about.
- Keep the speaker's own structuring language ("Now let me ask you something," "I want you
  to see something here") — it's part of what makes the compile feel authentic rather than
  ghostwritten.

# Compilation Prompt — Consolidated Transcripts → One Chronological Teaching Document

This is the prompt that produced a genuinely excellent result the first time (a 5-part
"Faith" sermon series compiled into one polished, chronologically-correct, voice-preserving
markdown document). Use it verbatim with placeholders filled in, against an LLM chat that
takes file attachments — or hand this whole file plus the transcripts to an agent with
Write access and ask it to follow §"Structural Rulebook" directly.

## What to attach

1. All N consolidated part-transcripts from `consolidate-transcripts.sh`
   (e.g. `Faith 1.txt` … `Faith 5.txt`).
2. Any broader-context recordings that cover the same material inside a wider session —
   e.g. full meeting/Google-Meet transcripts, if you have them. These aren't required, but
   they're what let the compiling model recover the *true* chronological order and connective
   context the numbered parts alone don't carry.

## The prompt (fill in the brackets)

```
Attached are transcripts of a series on [TOPIC] done by [TEACHER/SPEAKER NAME]
([N range, e.g. 1-5]).

After that, the attached are actual transcripts ([SOURCE, e.g. Google Meet]) from
which the [TOPIC] series was taught (broader in context as they cover entire
sessions as compared to the [N] parts that only cover the teaching).

From the above, generate (compile them into) one teaching on [TOPIC] by [TEACHER
NAME]. .md format. In the file, there should be a chronological flow of the
[TOPIC] series ([N range] doesn't really reflect the manner in which they were
taught — you might find that part 1 was taught after part 4). I think the [N
range] parts nail the teaching well, whereas the other transcripts sort of give
some context. If [TEACHER NAME] made any prayers/declarations/punchlines/
statements be sure to include them in the file, still in a chronological manner.
Also all scripture [or: quotes/citations from your authoritative source] to be
referenced in [NKJV, or your default translation/edition] unless of course
otherwise stated. Verify every citation against a real source rather than
relying on memory — including the chapter/verse number itself, not just the
wording. If [TEACHER NAME]'s spoken reference doesn't match what they're
quoting, don't just silently fix it: keep what they actually said as their own
words, and give the correct citation right alongside it. Format well —
headings, titles, bold, italic, etc.

This is a professional [TOPIC] document. Do not leave out a thing — that
includes not leaving out what was actually said, even a wrong reference number,
in favor of a silently "corrected" version. Let it be such that it is as if
[TEACHER NAME] is speaking directly to whoever reads it.

- **"be sure to include them ... still in a chronological manner"** — prayers/declarations/
  punchlines are exactly what a lazy summarizer drops first. Naming the category explicitly
  is what keeps them in.
- **"unless of course otherwise stated"** — the one correctly-scoped escape hatch: don't
  force the standard translation over a quote the speaker explicitly attributed elsewhere.
- **"Verify every citation against a real source rather than relying on memory"** — added
  after a real failure: a compiling model recalled "Romans 12:4" confidently and was wrong
  (the content quoted was Romans 2:4). Fluent, confident recall of a Bible reference is not
  verification. See "The Scripture Citation Rule" below for the exact pattern once you've
  verified — this phrase only covers *checking*, not *rendering*.

  right alongside it"** — completeness applies to the speaker's own words too, including their
  mistakes. A silently "corrected" citation deletes real information: what the speaker
  actually said, uncertainty and all. See the worked example below.

  a compile, not a digest. This now explicitly includes wrong-but-spoken citations, not just
  prayers/declarations/punchlines.
- **"as if [name] is speaking directly to whoever reads it"** — the instruction that produces
  first/second-person voice preservation instead of third-person academic paraphrase.

   Horizontal rule.

### Voice rules
- First person ("I") when the speaker refers to themself; second person ("you") when they
  address the audience directly. The reader should feel spoken to, not informed about.
- Keep the speaker's own structuring language ("Now let me ask you something," "I want you
  to see something here") — it's part of what makes the compile feel authentic rather than
  ghostwritten.

---

## The Scripture Citation Rule

Two failure modes, both wrong in opposite directions:

1. **Transcribing the speaker's spoken paraphrase as if it were the literal verse text.**
   (The original problem this rulebook already covered.)
2. **Silently "correcting" a misspoken chapter/verse number** — swapping in the right
   reference without showing that the speaker said something different. This looks tidier,
   but it deletes real information: what the speaker actually said, mistake and all. A
   reader (or the speaker themself, checking the document later) has no way to tell a
   verified correction from an invented one if corrections are invisible.

The fix for both is the same three-part pattern, and it requires the citation to have
actually been checked against a real source first (Method §5 in `skill.md` — not memory,
however confident):

1. Keep the speaker's own words — their paraphrase, and their spoken reference if they gave
   one, right or wrong — in the prose, attributed as what they said.
2. Immediately follow with the verified citation, in a normal scripture blockquote, supplying
   the real verse text.
3. Never present step 2 as if it were part of what the speaker said. It's the compiler
   supplying the real text, and the phrasing should make that clear (see example).

**Worked example** (a real case, from the "Emotional Intelligence" series, verified against
biblegateway.com/NKJV after the compiling model's first pass got the reference wrong from
memory):

> Pastor Charles introduced this as "the book of Romans, chapter 12 and verse 4" — the verse
> whose content he's actually quoting is Romans 2:4:
>
> > *"Or do you despise the riches of His goodness, forbearance, and longsuffering, not
> > knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?"*
> > — Romans 2:4 (NKJV)

Notice what this does *not* do: it doesn't pretend he said "2:4," and it doesn't present the
verified text as something he recited verbatim. It shows both — what was actually said, and
what's actually true — without erasing either one.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Periodic safe disk-usage check + cleanup + desktop notification.
# Runs every 5 min via the disk-cleanup.timer systemd --user unit.
set -uo pipefail

THRESHOLD=75
STATE_DIR="$HOME/.local/state/disk-cleanup"
LOCK_FILE="$STATE_DIR/run.lock"
LOG_FILE="$STATE_DIR/cleanup.log"
mkdir -p "$STATE_DIR"

log() { echo "$(date -Iseconds) $*" >> "$LOG_FILE"; }

exec 9>"$LOCK_FILE"
if ! flock -n 9; then
  log "skip: previous run still in progress"
  exit 0
fi

# rotate log once it grows past ~1MB
if [ -f "$LOG_FILE" ] && [ "$(stat -c%s "$LOG_FILE" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)" -gt 1048576 ]; then
  tail -n 500 "$LOG_FILE" > "$LOG_FILE.tmp" && mv "$LOG_FILE.tmp" "$LOG_FILE"
fi

usage_pct() { df --output=pcent / | tail -1 | tr -dc '0-9'; }
avail_kb()  { df --output=avail / | tail -1 | tr -dc '0-9'; }

HAVE_SUDO=0
sudo -n true 2>/dev/null && HAVE_SUDO=1

before_pct=$(usage_pct)
before_avail=$(avail_kb)
log "=== run start: usage ${before_pct}% ==="

CLEARED=()

step() {
  local desc="$1"; shift
  local b a freed
  b=$(avail_kb)
  if "$@" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1; then
    a=$(avail_kb)
    freed=$(( a - b ))
    if [ "$freed" -gt 1024 ]; then
      CLEARED+=("$desc (~$(( freed / 1024 ))MB)")
    fi
  else
    log "step failed (non-fatal): $desc"
  fi
}

# ---- user-space caches (no root needed) ----
clean_trash()    { rm -rf "$HOME"/.local/share/Trash/files/* "$HOME"/.local/share/Trash/info/* 2>/dev/null; }
clean_thumbs()   { find "$HOME/.cache/thumbnails" -type f -mtime +7 -delete 2>/dev/null; }
clean_browsers() {
  local d
  for d in "$HOME/.cache/google-chrome" "$HOME/.cache/BraveSoftware" "$HOME/.cache/chromium" \
           "$HOME"/.cache/mozilla/firefox/*/cache2 "$HOME/.cache/microsoft-edge"; do
    [ -d "$d" ] && find "$d" -mindepth 1 -delete 2>/dev/null
  done
  return 0
}
clean_pip()   { command -v pip  >/dev/null 2>&1 && pip cache purge; }
clean_npm()   { command -v npm  >/dev/null 2>&1 && npm cache clean --force; }
clean_yarn()  { command -v yarn >/dev/null 2>&1 && yarn cache clean; }
clean_go()    { command -v go   >/dev/null 2>&1 && go clean -cache; }
clean_cargo() { [ -d "$HOME/.cargo/registry/cache" ] && rm -rf "$HOME"/.cargo/registry/cache/*; return 0; }
clean_uv()    { [ -x "$HOME/.hermes/bin/uv" ] && "$HOME/.hermes/bin/uv" cache clean; }
clean_electron_cache() { [ -d "$HOME/.cache/electron" ] && rm -rf "$HOME"/.cache/electron/*; return 0; }

# ---- Hermes agent (~/.hermes): only its own regenerable caches/logs.
# sessions/, memories/, cron/, config.yaml, .env, SOUL.md, and the
# hermes-agent code checkout are NEVER touched by any step here.
clean_hermes_caches() {
  local d
  for d in "$HOME/.hermes/audio_cache" "$HOME/.hermes/image_cache"; do
    [ -d "$d" ] && find "$d" -type f -mtime +2 -delete 2>/dev/null
  done
  return 0
}
clean_hermes_pycache() {
  [ -d "$HOME/.hermes/hermes-agent" ] && \
    find "$HOME/.hermes/hermes-agent" -type d -name '__pycache__' -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null
  return 0
}
rotate_hermes_logs() {
  local f
  for f in "$HOME"/.hermes/logs/*.log "$HOME"/.hermes/logs/curator/*.log; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
    if [ "$(stat -c%s "$f" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)" -gt 5242880 ]; then
      tail -n 2000 "$f" > "$f.tmp" && mv "$f.tmp" "$f"
    fi
  done
  return 0
}
clean_hermes_misc_cache() {
  [ -d "$HOME/.hermes/cache" ] && find "$HOME/.hermes/cache" -type f -mtime +1 -delete 2>/dev/null
  [ -f "$HOME/.hermes/models_dev_cache.json" ] && \
    find "$HOME/.hermes/models_dev_cache.json" -mtime +1 -delete 2>/dev/null
  return 0
}
rotate_hermes_backups() {
  ls -t "$HOME"/.hermes/config.yaml.bak.* 2>/dev/null | tail -n +4 | xargs -r rm -f
  return 0
}

# ---- root-owned system caches ----
clean_tmp() {
  sudo find /tmp -mindepth 1 -mtime +1 \
    -not -path "/tmp/.X11-unix*" -not -path "/tmp/.ICE-unix*" \
    -not -path "/tmp/systemd-private-*" -not -path "*snap-private-tmp*" \
    -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null
  return 0
}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Periodic safe disk-usage check + cleanup + desktop notification.
# Runs every 5 min via the disk-cleanup.timer systemd --user unit.
set -uo pipefail

THRESHOLD=75
STATE_DIR="$HOME/.local/state/disk-cleanup"
LOCK_FILE="$STATE_DIR/run.lock"
LOG_FILE="$STATE_DIR/cleanup.log"
mkdir -p "$STATE_DIR"

log() { echo "$(date -Iseconds) $*" >> "$LOG_FILE"; }

exec 9>"$LOCK_FILE"
if ! flock -n 9; then
  log "skip: previous run still in progress"
  exit 0
fi

# rotate log once it grows past ~1MB
if [ -f "$LOG_FILE" ] && [ "$(stat -c%s "$LOG_FILE" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)" -gt 1048576 ]; then
  tail -n 500 "$LOG_FILE" > "$LOG_FILE.tmp" && mv "$LOG_FILE.tmp" "$LOG_FILE"
fi

usage_pct() { df --output=pcent / | tail -1 | tr -dc '0-9'; }
avail_kb()  { df --output=avail / | tail -1 | tr -dc '0-9'; }

HAVE_SUDO=0
sudo -n true 2>/dev/null && HAVE_SUDO=1

before_pct=$(usage_pct)
before_avail=$(avail_kb)
log "=== run start: usage ${before_pct}% ==="

CLEARED=()

step() {
  local desc="$1"; shift
  local b a freed
  b=$(avail_kb)
  if "$@" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1; then
    a=$(avail_kb)
    freed=$(( a - b ))
    if [ "$freed" -gt 1024 ]; then
      CLEARED+=("$desc (~$(( freed / 1024 ))MB)")
    fi
  else
    log "step failed (non-fatal): $desc"
  fi
}

clean_thumbs()   { find "$HOME/.cache/thumbnails" -type f -mtime +7 -delete 2>/dev/null; }

    [ -d "$d" ] && find "$d" -mindepth 1 -delete 2>/dev/null
  done
  return 0
}

clean_npm()   { command -v npm  >/dev/null 2>&1 && npm cache clean --force; }
clean_yarn()  { command -v yarn >/dev/null 2>&1 && yarn cache clean; }
clean_go()    { command -v go   >/dev/null 2>&1 && go clean -cache; }
clean_cargo() { [ -d "$HOME/.cargo/registry/cache" ] && rm -rf "$HOME"/.cargo/registry/cache/*; return 0; }
clean_uv()    { [ -x "$HOME/.hermes/bin/uv" ] && "$HOME/.hermes/bin/uv" cache clean; }
clean_electron_cache() { [ -d "$HOME/.cache/electron" ] && rm -rf "$HOME"/.cache/electron/*; return 0; }

  return 0

rotate_hermes_logs() {
  local f

  return 0

clean_hermes_misc_cache() {
  [ -d "$HOME/.hermes/cache" ] && find "$HOME/.hermes/cache" -type f -mtime +1 -delete 2>/dev/null
  [ -f "$HOME/.hermes/models_dev_cache.json" ] && \
    find "$HOME/.hermes/models_dev_cache.json" -mtime +1 -delete 2>/dev/null
  return 0

rotate_hermes_backups() {
  ls -t "$HOME"/.hermes/config.yaml.bak.* 2>/dev/null | tail -n +4 | xargs -r rm -f

clean_browsers() {
  local d
  for d in "$HOME/.cache/google-chrome" "$HOME/.cache/BraveSoftware" "$HOME/.cache/chromium" \
           "$HOME"/.cache/mozilla/firefox/*/cache2 "$HOME/.cache/microsoft-edge"; do
    [ -d "$d" ] && find "$d" -mindepth 1 -delete 2>/dev/null
  done
  return 0
}
# Chromium-family browsers (Brave, Chrome, Chromium, Edge) keep their real,
# regenerable disk caches INSIDE the profile under ~/.config/<vendor>/<product>/,
# not under ~/.cache — clean_browsers() above only ever hit an empty path for
# these. Found via audit: Brave-Browser-Beta's Service Worker cache alone was
# 691M, on a 7.7G disk, silently never touched by any prior cleanup step.
# ONLY touches known-regenerable cache subdirs, both at the browser-root level
# and per-profile. Deliberately never touches: Extensions (installed code),
# IndexedDB/File System/Local Extension Settings (real site & extension data),
# History/Cookies/Sessions/Preferences/Web Data/Local Storage/Session Storage/
# Favicons (real browser state — touching these would sign the user out of
# sites, lose saved logins/autofill, lose open tabs, or reset extensions).
clean_chromium_profile_caches() {
  local base profile
  for base in "$HOME/.config/BraveSoftware/Brave-Browser-Beta" \
              "$HOME/.config/BraveSoftware/Brave-Browser" \
              "$HOME/.config/google-chrome" "$HOME/.config/chromium" \
              "$HOME/.config/microsoft-edge"; do
    [ -d "$base" ] || continue
    for d in "$base/GPUPersistentCache" "$base/component_crx_cache" "$base/Safe Browsing"; do
      [ -d "$d" ] && find "$d" -mindepth 1 -delete 2>/dev/null
    done
    for profile in "$base"/Default "$base"/Profile\ *; do
      [ -d "$profile" ] || continue
      for d in "Service Worker" "GPUCache" "Code Cache" "DawnWebGPUCache" "DawnGraphiteCache"; do
        [ -d "$profile/$d" ] && rm -rf "${profile:?}/${d:?}" 2>/dev/null
      done
    done
  done
  return 0
}
# The Claude CLI's self-updater (~/.local/share/claude/versions/<ver>) does
# not clean up its own old versions — found via audit: two full copies
# (2.1.235 + 2.1.237, ~330M each) sitting side by side, only one in use.
# This recurs on every auto-update, so it needs to be a permanent step, not
# a one-off delete. Only ever removes versions OTHER than the one the
# ~/.local/bin/claude symlink currently resolves to.
clean_stale_claude_versions() {
  local versions_dir="$HOME/.local/share/claude/versions"
  local claude_bin
  claude_bin=$(command -v claude 2>/dev/null) || return 0
  [ -d "$versions_dir" ] || return 0
  local active
  active=$(readlink -f "$claude_bin" 2>/dev/null) || return 0
  local f base
  for f in "$versions_dir"/*; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
    [ "$f" = "$active" ] && continue
    base=$(basename "$f")
    rm -f "$f" "$HOME/.local/state/claude/locks/$base.lock" 2>/dev/null
  done
  return 0
}

toolUseResult.originalFile:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Periodic safe disk-usage check + cleanup + desktop notification.
# Runs every 5 min via the disk-cleanup.timer systemd --user unit.
set -uo pipefail

THRESHOLD=75
STATE_DIR="$HOME/.local/state/disk-cleanup"
LOCK_FILE="$STATE_DIR/run.lock"
LOG_FILE="$STATE_DIR/cleanup.log"
mkdir -p "$STATE_DIR"

log() { echo "$(date -Iseconds) $*" >> "$LOG_FILE"; }

exec 9>"$LOCK_FILE"
if ! flock -n 9; then
  log "skip: previous run still in progress"
  exit 0
fi

# rotate log once it grows past ~1MB
if [ -f "$LOG_FILE" ] && [ "$(stat -c%s "$LOG_FILE" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)" -gt 1048576 ]; then
  tail -n 500 "$LOG_FILE" > "$LOG_FILE.tmp" && mv "$LOG_FILE.tmp" "$LOG_FILE"
fi

usage_pct() { df --output=pcent / | tail -1 | tr -dc '0-9'; }
avail_kb()  { df --output=avail / | tail -1 | tr -dc '0-9'; }

HAVE_SUDO=0
sudo -n true 2>/dev/null && HAVE_SUDO=1

before_pct=$(usage_pct)
before_avail=$(avail_kb)
log "=== run start: usage ${before_pct}% ==="

CLEARED=()

step() {
  local desc="$1"; shift
  local b a freed
  b=$(avail_kb)
  if "$@" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1; then
    a=$(avail_kb)
    freed=$(( a - b ))
    if [ "$freed" -gt 1024 ]; then
      CLEARED+=("$desc (~$(( freed / 1024 ))MB)")
    fi
  else
    log "step failed (non-fatal): $desc"
  fi
}

# ---- user-space caches (no root needed) ----
clean_trash()    { rm -rf "$HOME"/.local/share/Trash/files/* "$HOME"/.local/share/Trash/info/* 2>/dev/null; }
clean_thumbs()   { find "$HOME/.cache/thumbnails" -type f -mtime +7 -delete 2>/dev/null; }
clean_browsers() {
  local d
  for d in "$HOME/.cache/google-chrome" "$HOME/.cache/BraveSoftware" "$HOME/.cache/chromium" \
           "$HOME"/.cache/mozilla/firefox/*/cache2 "$HOME/.cache/microsoft-edge"; do
    [ -d "$d" ] && find "$d" -mindepth 1 -delete 2>/dev/null
  done
  return 0
}
clean_pip()   { command -v pip  >/dev/null 2>&1 && pip cache purge; }
clean_npm()   { command -v npm  >/dev/null 2>&1 && npm cache clean --force; }
clean_yarn()  { command -v yarn >/dev/null 2>&1 && yarn cache clean; }
clean_go()    { command -v go   >/dev/null 2>&1 && go clean -cache; }
clean_cargo() { [ -d "$HOME/.cargo/registry/cache" ] && rm -rf "$HOME"/.cargo/registry/cache/*; return 0; }
clean_uv()    { [ -x "$HOME/.hermes/bin/uv" ] && "$HOME/.hermes/bin/uv" cache clean; }
clean_electron_cache() { [ -d "$HOME/.cache/electron" ] && rm -rf "$HOME"/.cache/electron/*; return 0; }

# ---- Hermes agent (~/.hermes): only its own regenerable caches/logs.
# sessions/, memories/, cron/, config.yaml, .env, SOUL.md, and the
# hermes-agent code checkout are NEVER touched by any step here.
clean_hermes_caches() {
  local d
  for d in "$HOME/.hermes/audio_cache" "$HOME/.hermes/image_cache"; do
    [ -d "$d" ] && find "$d" -type f -mtime +2 -delete 2>/dev/null
  done
  return 0
}
clean_hermes_pycache() {
  [ -d "$HOME/.hermes/hermes-agent" ] && \
    find "$HOME/.hermes/hermes-agent" -type d -name '__pycache__' -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null
  return 0
}
rotate_hermes_logs() {
  local f
  for f in "$HOME"/.hermes/logs/*.log "$HOME"/.hermes/logs/curator/*.log; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
    if [ "$(stat -c%s "$f" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)" -gt 5242880 ]; then
      tail -n 2000 "$f" > "$f.tmp" && mv "$f.tmp" "$f"
    fi
  done
  return 0
}
clean_hermes_misc_cache() {
  [ -d "$HOME/.hermes/cache" ] && find "$HOME/.hermes/cache" -type f -mtime +1 -delete 2>/dev/null
  [ -f "$HOME/.hermes/models_dev_cache.json" ] && \
    find "$HOME/.hermes/models_dev_cache.json" -mtime +1 -delete 2>/dev/null
  return 0
}
rotate_hermes_backups() {
  ls -t "$HOME"/.hermes/config.yaml.bak.* 2>/dev/null | tail -n +4 | xargs -r rm -f
  return 0
}

# ---- root-owned system caches ----
clean_tmp() {
  sudo find /tmp -mindepth 1 -mtime +1 \
    -not -path "/tmp/.X11-unix*" -not -path "/tmp/.ICE-unix*" \
    -not -path "/tmp/systemd-private-*" -not -path "*snap-private-tmp*" \
    -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null
  return 0
}
clean_coredumps() { sudo find /var/crash /var/lib/systemd/coredump -type f -mtime +1 -delete 2>/dev/null; return 0; }
clean_snap_old() {
  snap list --all 2>/dev/null | awk '/disabled/{print $1, $3}' | \
    while read -r name rev; do sudo snap remove "$name" --revision="$rev" >/dev/null 2>&1; done
  return 0
}
clean_apt_index_cache() { sudo rm -f /var/cache/apt/pkgcache.bin /var/cache/apt/srcpkgcache.bin; return 0; }
clean_docker() { sudo docker system prune -f; }
clean_podman() { podman system prune -f; }
deep_journal_vacuum() { sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=6h; }
deep_tmp_sweep() {
  sudo find /tmp -mindepth 1 -mmin +180 \
    -not -path "/tmp/.X11-unix*" -not -path "/tmp/.ICE-unix*" \
    -not -path "/tmp/systemd-private-*" -not -path "*snap-private-tmp*" \
    -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null
  return 0
}
top_consumers() {
  du -sh "$HOME/.hermes" "$HOME/.cache" "$HOME/.npm" "$HOME/.cargo" \
    /var/cache/apt/archives 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -5
}

step "Trash"           clean_trash
step "Thumbnail cache"  clean_thumbs
step "Browser caches"   clean_browsers
step "pip cache"        clean_pip
step "npm cache"        clean_npm
step "yarn cache"       clean_yarn
step "Go build cache"   clean_go
step "Cargo registry cache" clean_cargo
step "uv package cache" clean_uv
step "Electron download cache" clean_electron_cache
step "Hermes audio/image cache (>2d)" clean_hermes_caches
step "Hermes __pycache__"      clean_hermes_pycache
step "Hermes log rotation (>5MB)" rotate_hermes_logs
step "Hermes misc cache (>1d)" clean_hermes_misc_cache
step "Hermes config backups (keep 3)" rotate_hermes_backups

if systemctl --user is-active --quiet hermes-gateway.service 2>/dev/null; then
  :
elif systemctl --user list-unit-files hermes-gateway.service >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  log "warning: hermes-gateway.service is installed but not active"
fi

if [ "$HAVE_SUDO" -eq 1 ]; then
  step "APT package cache"        sudo apt-get clean
  step "APT autoclean"            sudo apt-get autoclean -y
  step "APT index cache"          clean_apt_index_cache
  step "systemd journal (>2d)"    sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=2d
  step "Old core dumps"           clean_coredumps
  step "Orphaned /tmp files (>1d)" clean_tmp
  command -v snap    >/dev/null 2>&1 && step "Old snap revisions"       clean_snap_old
  command -v flatpak >/dev/null 2>&1 && step "Unused flatpak runtimes"  flatpak uninstall --unused -y
  if command -v docker >/dev/null 2>&1 && sudo docker info >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    step "Unused docker data" clean_docker
  fi
  command -v podman  >/dev/null 2>&1 && step "Unused podman data"       clean_podman
else
  log "no passwordless sudo: skipped root-owned cleanup steps"
fi

EMERGENCY_FLOOR_KB=400000
if [ "$HAVE_SUDO" -eq 1 ] && [ "$(avail_kb)" -lt "$EMERGENCY_FLOOR_KB" ]; then
  log "EMERGENCY: free space under 400MB after standard cleanup — running deeper pass"
  step "Deep journal vacuum (>6h)" deep_journal_vacuum
  step "Deep /tmp sweep (>3h)"     deep_tmp_sweep
fi

after_pct=$(usage_pct)
after_avail=$(avail_kb)
freed_total_mb=$(( (after_avail - before_avail) / 1024 ))
log "=== run end: usage ${after_pct}% (freed ${freed_total_mb}MB) ==="

if [ "${#CLEARED[@]}" -eq 0 ]; then

content.text:
## Due diligence findings

Used the same "genuinely new since boot" technique from our earlier session (`find / -xdev -newer <boot-time>`, since naive `du` on this overlay counts the whole squashfs base too). Two real problems turned up — both **bugs in the existing script**, not just normal bloat:

1. **Brave-Beta's actual cache was never being cleared.** The script's `clean_browsers()` only targeted `~/.cache/BraveSoftware` — but Chromium-family browsers keep their real disk cache *inside the profile* under `~/.config/BraveSoftware/Brave-Browser-Beta/Default/...`. That path was silently empty the whole time while `Service Worker/` cache alone had grown to **691MB**, completely untouched, run after run.
2. **The Claude CLI's self-updater never cleans up old versions.** `~/.local/share/claude/versions/` had two full ~330MB copies (2.1.235 and 2.1.237) sitting side by side — only the symlinked one is ever in use. This recurs on every auto-update, and nothing was pruning it.

Everything else checked out as legitimate: Hermes agent (2.2GB — venv + node_modules, previously confirmed as real), `~/Downloads` (255MB, your own files), journal (80MB, already in check).

## What I refined in `~/bin/disk-cleanup.sh`

- Added `clean_chromium_profile_caches()` — clears only the verified-regenerable cache dirs (`Service Worker`, `GPUCache`, `Code Cache`, Dawn shader caches, `component_crx_cache`, `Safe Browsing`, `GPUPersistentCache`) across Brave-Beta/Brave/Chrome/Chromium/Edge, whatever's present. Explicitly never touches `Extensions`, `IndexedDB`, `Local Extension Settings`, `History`, `Cookies`, `Sessions`, `Preferences`, `Web Data`, or `Local/Session Storage` — that's real state (logins, bookmarks, open tabs, installed extensions), not cache.
- Added `clean_stale_claude_versions()` — resolves the active version via the `~/.local/bin/claude` symlink and removes every *other* version directory (and its stale lock file). Runs every 5 minutes going forward, so this won't re-accumulate.
- Updated the `top_consumers()` diagnostic to actually include Brave and Downloads, so future critical alerts show the real picture instead of missing the biggest item.

## Verified live

Ran it for real (not a dry run): **82% → 73% used, ~1GB reclaimed**, confirmed via `df` before/after and by checking the Brave cache dirs and `versions/` folder directly afterward (only `2.1.237` remains). Brave is still running fine — these are pure disk caches, safe to clear live. The 5-minute systemd timer has been active continuously since Aug 18 and picked up the fix on its very next run.

Nothing else worth automating further right now — the remaining 5.6GB used is genuinely Hermes, installed tools, and your own files, not garbage.

There's two projects on  my repos; caspahub & caspahub-booking here's some context on how I/we have come with the two; # CaspaHub — Complete Agent Context Document

> **Purpose:** This document gives a Claude Code agent (or any incoming contributor) the full picture of CaspaHub — what was built, why decisions were made, what exists in the repos today, what is broken, and what needs to happen next. It is written as a living context document, not a summary. Read it fully before touching any code.
>
> **Date compiled:** August 20, 2026
> **Compiled from:** Full conversation history, codebase audits (August 17, 2026), screen/flow audit, competitor teardown (carwash.co.ke, August 13, 2026), executive platform report, all PRDs, Thomas Mweri's directive.
>
> **Founders:** Kennedy Muritu (Ken) — developer/technical lead | Thomas Kaingu Mweri (Tom) — co-founder, business
> **Immediate directive from Tom:** Q3 must not end with nothing testable in market. A DRB/guide with timelines is needed. The MVP must ship.

---

## PART 1 — WHAT CASPAHUB IS

### The Business

CaspaHub is a **two-sided vehicle care platform** for East Africa, starting with car washes in Kenya.

**Side 1 — Operator OS (B2B SaaS):**
Car wash businesses pay a monthly subscription to manage bookings, queue, staff, commissions, payments, loyalty, and analytics from a single dashboard.

**Side 2 — Consumer Marketplace (B2C):**
Car owners find nearby washes, book, pay with M-Pesa, and track their wash in real time — for free.

**The analogy that explains it:** Uber manages drivers and routes (B2B infrastructure) but the real product is the rider experience (B2C). Similarly, CaspaHub manages car wash operators but the real product is the car owner experience. The operator tool creates supply. The consumer app creates demand. Both sides need each other.

**The long-term vision:** CaspaHub becomes the transaction and engagement layer for all vehicle care businesses in East Africa — starting with car washes, expanding to tyre centres, oil change shops, garages, and EV charging stations.

### The Market Context

- Kenya has **4.97 million registered motor vehicles** (2024), growing ~8% annually
- ~**40,000 car washes** in Kenya — zero vertical SaaS serving them
- **97% M-Pesa adoption** — payments are solved
- **One direct competitor exists:** carwash.co.ke (built by JBing Systems Ltd, Embu) — live on Play Store, has 5 locations, is essentially a booking form with SMS confirmation. No map, no real-time tracking, no loyalty, no operator dashboard, no trust signals, no policies. Well below what CaspaHub is building. A full UX teardown was done on August 13, 2026 — see Part 5.
- **Global car wash app market:** $1.47B in 2025, projected $5B by 2035 at 13.1% CAGR

### The Go-To-Market Strategy

**Wedge:** Launch as a booking platform first. Simple enough for an operator to say yes to in one conversation. Use real bookings to get inside car washes, collect pain point data, then expand features based on what operators actually ask for.

This is not a pivot — it's a thin-wedge entry. The full platform stays. The booking MVP is the door.

**Tom's survey form** (designed by Thomas) is the demand validation instrument. It covers 7 sections: business profile, operational pain points, financial tracking, customer management, technology adoption, app value proposition, and final thoughts. A short 5-question cold version should precede the full form for new contacts.

---

## PART 2 — THE TWO REPOSITORIES

There are **two separate GitHub repositories** under `ken-muritu/`:

### Repository 1: `ken-muritu/caspahub` (Operator Platform)

The main, actively developed platform. **~267 files.** This is the operator OS.

**Stack:**
- Next.js 16.2.9, App Router, React 19.2.4, TypeScript 5
- Drizzle ORM 0.45.2 over Turso/libSQL
- Auth.js (NextAuth) v5 beta, bcryptjs (cost factor 12)
- @radix-ui/* full component kit
- Sentry, recharts, react-hook-form, jsbarcode, idb (IndexedDB), uuid
- Serwist (PWA/service worker)
- PayHero (M-Pesa aggregator)
- Vercel deployment

**Database architecture — critical to understand:**
- **One shared metadata database** (Turso): tenants, plans, subscriptions, global users, memberships, invitations, audit logs, notification queue, push subscriptions, platform support tickets, compliance requests
- **One isolated Turso database per tenant** (per car wash business), provisioned on signup via the Turso Cloud API. Each tenant DB contains: branches, washServices, washBookings, washBookingEvents, users (staff), shifts, conversations, messages, and 13 pharmacy/clinic legacy tables (inherited from the Solera fork — unused, known dead weight)
- Tenant DB tokens encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM), auto-rotate at ~90-day TTL
- `src/lib/tenant.ts` (23.6KB) is the central orchestrator

**Routing structure:**
- `(app)` — operator dashboard (bookings, queue, customers, staff, fleet, payments, loyalty, analytics, settings, messages)
- `(auth)` — sign-in, sign-up, email verification, password reset
- Public marketing routes — homepage, pricing, FAQ, contact, legal
- Consumer booking flow (public, cross-tenant) — `/find`, `/book/[branchId]`, `/track/[bookingId]`, `/profile`, `/onboarding`
- Platform admin console — gated to `PLATFORM_ADMIN_EMAILS`

**RBAC:** 7 roles (`super_admin, admin, manager, supervisor, attendant, cashier, consumer`) × 14 modules × 4 actions. Enforced at middleware and server action level.

**Booking state machine (event-sourced — critical pattern):**
```
BOOKED → QUEUED → BAY_ASSIGNED → WASHING → READY → COMPLETED
                                                    ↘ CANCELLED
```
Status is NEVER stored as a mutable column. Every status change is an `INSERT` into `washBookingEvents`. Current status = the latest event row. This is the most important architectural decision in the platform.

**Payments:**

## PART 3 — ARCHITECTURE DECISIONS (AND WHY)

### Why Turso over Supabase

Supabase was initially wired (`lib/supabase.ts`, `lib/supabase-server.ts`) but never activated — no data, no RLS, no auth flows in production. Decision to move to Turso was made before any Supabase data existed, making it a clean swap.

Reasons:
1. **FARIS proof** — Ken built FARIS (petrol station management SaaS) on Turso + Prisma/Drizzle. It's live, working, proven. CaspaHub inherits the same patterns.
2. **DB-per-tenant model** — SQLite per tenant is natural isolation without RLS complexity. Each car wash gets its own isolated database.
3. **Edge reads** — Turso replicates to 35+ edge regions. Kenya latency matters.
4. **Cost** — Supabase free → paid tier jump is steep. Turso free tier is generous at early stage.
5. **Local dev** — `file:./dev.db` works offline, instantly. No Docker, no cloud project needed.

Tradeoff accepted: No built-in Realtime (Supabase channel) → replaced with 5–8 second polling on tracker. Viable for MVP.

### Why `BookingEvent` is append-only (the most important decision)

**Rule: Never `UPDATE` a booking's status. Always `INSERT` a new `BookingEvent` row.**

Current status = latest row in `washBookingEvents` ordered by `createdAt` DESC.

This gives for free: full audit trail, dispute resolution timestamps, analytics per stage, AI query readiness, real-time tracker state, notification triggers. FARIS uses the same pattern for shift stock snapshots. It is non-negotiable.

### Why `Customer` is platform-level (no `organizationId`)

A car owner may book at Wash A today and Wash B next week. If `Customer` had an `organizationId`, the marketplace breaks — the same person appears as a different customer at every wash. The correct model: `Customer` and `Vehicle` are platform-level (no tenant scope). `Booking` carries both `organizationId` (the wash) and `customerId` (the person). This is the join point.

### Why two repos, not one monorepo

`caspahub` (operator) and `caspahub-booking` (consumer) are separate Next.js apps deployed to separate Vercel projects. They share infrastructure (same Turso DBs, same auth secret, same PayHero, same Stream app) but are independently deployable, independently scalable, and independently maintainable. The operator app is multi-tenant SaaS. The consumer app is a public-facing PWA. Separating them keeps each codebase focused.

### Why PayHero over Daraja direct

PayHero is a Kenyan M-Pesa aggregator (like a middleware between the app and Safaricom). It handles STK Push initiation, callback normalization, and some edge cases around double-callbacks. The Daraja direct integration in `caspahub` (`src/app/api/mpesa/callback/route.ts`) always returns HTTP 501 — it's dead scaffolding. All live payment flow goes through PayHero.

## PART 4 — WHAT HAS BEEN STUDIED AND DECIDED

### FARIS (the proof of concept)

Ken built FARIS — a petrol station management system — using the exact same stack: Turso + Drizzle/Prisma, NextAuth v5, bcrypt, non-blocking alerts (copy of `lib/notify.ts`), CI/CD backups. It's live and working. CaspaHub's backend architecture is directly informed by FARIS's patterns.

Key FARIS patterns carried into CaspaHub:
- Singleton DB client with LibSQL adapter
- bcrypt cost factor 12, login lockout (5 attempts / 15 min)
- `mustChangePwd` flag + proxy.ts redirect
- Append-only event sourcing for operational records
- Non-blocking notifications (commit first, notify after)
- Daily Turso backup via GitHub Actions

### Connecteam (marketing site reference)

Studied Connecteam's homepage and pricing architecture as a model for how to structure CaspaHub's operator-facing marketing site. Key learnings:
- Marketing site completely separate from SaaS app — marketing converts, product lives at `app.connecteam.com`
- Features grouped by job-to-be-done (not by technical capability)
- Hub-based pricing with clear feature gates
- 14-day trial, no credit card, free tier for small operators
- Heavy social proof architecture (logos, testimonials, metrics)

### carwash.co.ke (direct competitor — full teardown done)

Teardown conducted August 13, 2026. Key findings:

**What they do right:** Fast load (~694ms DOM-complete), clean mobile responsive, guest booking (no login required), clear package pricing (KES 200 / 350 / 350 / 500), vehicle type selection (CAR/SUV/VAN/BUS/LORRY/MOTORBIKE), SMS confirmation, booking reference tracking.

**What they fail at (CaspaHub's opportunities):**
- **Critical bug:** Homepage retains selected-carwash state after navigation, corrupting footer contact/social info
- No map or pin visualization in discovery
- Free-form time input not connected to capacity, queue, or opening hours
- Payment method never disclosed anywhere in booking flow
- No cancellation, no-show, refund, or change policy
- All 5 locations show identical packages/prices — no differentiation
- No photos, ratings, reviews, hours on location profiles
- No loyalty, no subscriptions, no push notifications, no WhatsApp
- 5-day booking cap invisible until user tries
- No Terms of Service, Privacy Policy, Refund Policy — serious trust gap
- `/login`, `/admin`, `/dashboard` silently redirect to homepage with no explanation
- Commercial terms (subscription fees, commissions) hidden from operators before signup

**Strategic summary:** carwash.co.ke is a booking form with SMS. CaspaHub, built to spec, is a product. Every weakness in their teardown is a feature on CaspaHub's roadmap.

### Uber UX patterns (screen/flow audit done August 17, 2026)

Full audit of 41 Uber rider app screenshots + 20 unique website states. Key decision: **CaspaHub is not Uber.** Uber manages a moving second party (driver). CaspaHub has a fixed location (the carwash). This eliminates: live driver GPS tracking, pickup-pin placement, driver-nearby alerts, PIN-to-verify-car, auto-rematch.

What CaspaHub replaces these with:
- Queue/bay status instead of driver tracking
- "Your car is ready" push instead of "driver nearby"
- Single-field location search instead of pickup+dropoff
- Booking tracker with stage illustrations instead of map route

What CaspaHub reuses from Uber: auth flows, wallet/payments, settings screens, family/household profiles, bottom tab nav structure, account screen layout.

## PART 9 — WHAT TO NEVER DO

These are non-negotiable rules derived from months of decisions and mistakes. Do not violate them.

1. **Never UPDATE booking status directly.** Always INSERT a new `washBookingEvents` row. Current status = latest event. This is the entire audit trail.

2. **Never apply `organizationId` to `Customer` or `Vehicle` tables.** They are platform-level. `Booking` is the join point.

3. **Never build UI before the API exists.** Schema first. API route second. UI third.

4. **Never accept a Daraja/PayHero callback without checking idempotency first.** M-Pesa callbacks arrive twice. Check `checkoutRequestId` before processing.

5. **Never make mock data permanent.** Every hardcoded value is technical debt with a deadline. Seed real data.

6. **Never add features from the out-of-scope list (Part 6).** Subscriptions, loyalty points, APK, Swahili, AI — these are v1.1. Do not scope creep.

7. **Never touch `/api/branches` without adding caching.** The fan-out to every tenant DB on every request is a scaling risk. Any work on this route must include response caching (minimum: Next.js `revalidate: 30`).

8. **Never deploy without environment variable validation.** The app should throw on missing required vars in production. This is already implemented — do not remove it.

9. **Never leave dead code in place.** `src/lib/actions/carwash.ts` and `src/lib/actions/pharmacy.ts` in the `caspahub` repo are confirmed dead (byte-identical, unimported, pharmacy logic in a carwash file). Delete them when touching that codebase.

10. **Never add a feature without an empty state, error state, and loading skeleton.** Every data-fetching UI must handle all three.

input.content:
# CaspaHub — Due Diligence & Repo Verification Report

**Date:** August 20, 2026
**Method:** Direct audit of `ken-muritu/caspahub` and `ken-muritu/caspahub-booking` (both cloned fresh from GitHub, `main` branch, latest commit each dated **2026-08-18**), cross-checked line-by-line against the attached "CaspaHub — Complete Agent Context Document." Every claim below was checked against actual source — file hashes, grep results, live HTTP requests — not re-derived from the same conversation history the original document came from.

**Bottom line up front:** The architecture, stack, and bug findings in the context document are **almost entirely accurate** — genuinely good, verifiable work. But **the `caspahub-booking` "what's missing" section is significantly stale.** Both repos picked up real commits on **August 18**, after the document's context was compiled, and most of the Week 1–3 sprint items in Part 5 are **already built and live**. If the 6-week sprint plan is run as written, roughly the first two weeks would be spent re-building things that already exist. That's the single most important thing this report has to tell you.

---

## 1. What's Confirmed Accurate

Everything in this section was checked directly and matches the document.

### Stack & versions
- `caspahub`: Next.js `16.2.9`, React `19.2.4`, TypeScript `^5`, `drizzle-orm ^0.45.2`, `next-auth ^5.0.0-beta.31`, `bcryptjs ^3.0.3`, `@sentry/nextjs`, `recharts`, `react-hook-form`, `jsbarcode`, `idb`, `uuid`, `@serwist/next` — all confirmed present and at the stated versions.
- `caspahub-booking`: same base versions, plus `leaflet ^1.9.4`, `react-leaflet ^5.0.0`, `stream-chat`, `web-push`, `zustand` — confirmed.
- **One nuance the document doesn't mention:** `stream-chat`, `stream-chat-react`, `web-push`, and `zustand` are *also* dependencies of `caspahub` itself, not exclusive to `caspahub-booking` as the "plus:" framing in Part 2 implies. This is consistent with the document's own note that GetStream is "partially wired server-side" in `caspahub` — just worth knowing it's not a clean stack split.

### Database architecture
- `src/lib/tenant.ts` is **23,644 bytes** — the document's "23.6KB" is exact, not rounded.
- Metadata DB (`src/db/schema/metadata.ts`) has 14 tables, all matching the document's description (tenants, plans, subscriptions, globalUsers, tenantMemberships, tenantInvitations, auditLogs, notificationQueue, pushSubscriptions, platformSupportTickets, complianceRequests, plus onboardingLocks and profileChangeRequests and platformSupportMessages, which the document doesn't name but doesn't contradict either).
- **13 pharmacy/clinic legacy tables** in the tenant schema — this exact count is confirmed: `categories, suppliers, products, inventoryBatches, patients, prescriptions, prescriptionItems, appointments, consultations, vitals, patientConsents, sales, saleItems`.

### Confirmed bugs (all verified against actual source, not just described)
| Claim | Verified | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `syncBookingPayment` is dead code | ✅ Exact | Defined once in `wash.ts:210`, zero other references anywhere in `src/` |
| PayHero webhook uses `confirmBookingPayment` instead | ✅ Exact | `payhero/callback/route.ts` imports and calls it; the two functions are genuinely separate code paths |
